from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: The Reynolds Number (Re)", [
            "Turbulence is flow chaos transition.", 
            "Reynolds Number balances inertia versus viscosity.", 
            "Low Re is smooth laminar flow.", 
            "High Re creates chaotic vortices.", 
            "Formula: Re equals rho v L over mu."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        re_label = Text("Reynolds Number (Re)", font_size=36, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(re_label, 'B2')
        self.play(FadeIn(re_label))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        
        # Define formula parts separately for potential highlighting
        formula = MathTex(r"Re", "=", r"{\rho v L \over \mu}", color="#FFD700")
        self.place_at_grid(formula, 'C3', scale_factor=1.5)
        self.play(Write(formula))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        # No specific visual action required by storyboard, just transition.

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(BLUE))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        # Flash variables
        # Note: MathTex split into submobjects: 0:'Re', 1:'=', 2:fraction part.
        # Inside the fraction (index 2), the structure is usually: [numerator, bar, denominator]
        # Accessing indices safely based on typical MathTex splitting
        self.play(Indicate(formula[0], color=RED), run_time=1)
        self.play(Indicate(formula[2][0], color=RED), run_time=1)
        self.play(Indicate(formula[2][2], color=RED), run_time=1)
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Energy follows -5/3 power law.",
            "Plot log energy versus wave number.",
            "Slope -5/3 marks inertial range.",
            "Eddies are self-similar fractal structures.",
            "Geometry repeats across scale ranges."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Mathematical Structure: The -5/3 Power Law", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        eq = MathTex(r"E(k) = C \epsilon^{2/3} k^{-5/3}", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(eq, 'B2', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(Write(eq))
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        axes = Axes(x_range=[0, 3, 1], y_range=[0, 3, 1], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        plot = axes.plot(lambda x: 3 - x, x_range=[0.5, 2.5], color=BLUE)
        graph = VGroup(axes, plot)
        self.place_in_area(graph, 'D1', 'F6', scale_factor=0.6)
        self.play(Create(axes), Create(plot))
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        slope_label = MathTex(r"slope = -5/3", color=RED).scale(0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(slope_label, 'C5')
        self.play(Write(slope_label))
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Representing fractal/self-similarity with simple repeating structure
        circle = Circle(radius=0.5, color=GREEN)
        self.place_at_grid(circle, 'B5', scale_factor=0.5)
        self.play(GrowFromCenter(circle))
        self.lecture[3].set_color(YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        circle2 = Circle(radius=0.25, color=GREEN)
        self.place_at_grid(circle2, 'B6', scale_factor=0.5)
        self.play(GrowFromCenter(circle2))
        self.lecture[4].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: Fundamental Constants and Mathematical Structure in Turbulence

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Reynolds Number (Re)
sections.content: Define turbulence as a transition from laminar flow. Introduce the Reynolds Number (Re = ρvL/μ) as the dimensionless ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces. Use a visual 'speed gauge' animation transitioning from smooth fluid layers to chaotic vortices as Re increases.
sections.example: A toy submarine moving through a pool: slow motion (low Re) shows smooth flow lines; rapid acceleration (high Re) triggers wake vortices.

sections.title: The Kolmogorov Cascade & Universal Constants
sections.content: Explain energy transfer from large-scale eddies to small-scale dissipation via the 'Richardson Cascade.' Introduce the Kolmogorov constant (C ≈ 1.5) as the universal scaling factor that links energy dissipation rate (ε) to the spectrum of turbulence.
sections.example: A whirlpool in a bathtub: the large swirling vortex breaking down into smaller, spinning foam-bubbles until they vanish into microscopic heat.

sections.title: The Mathematical Structure: The -5/3 Power Law
sections.content: Present the Kolmogorov -5/3 spectrum. Graphically demonstrate a log-log plot of Energy Density (E) vs. Wave Number (k). Show how the slope of -5/3 emerges in the 'inertial range,' representing the self-similar structure of eddies.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'fractal' tree: each branch splits into smaller branches following a self-similar ratio, just as large eddies break into geometrically similar smaller eddies.

sections.title: Application: Why Constant Matters
sections.content: Summarize how these mathematical constants allow us to predict high-speed turbulence (which is otherwise uncomputable) by modeling the universal inertial range. Emphasize that these constants hold true regardless of the fluid (air vs. water).
sections.example: An aerospace engineer using the -5/3 power law to predict drag forces on a jet engine's turbine blade, allowing the engine to run without melting.
